what_its_for: Cefpodoxime is an antibiotic used to treat certain bacterial infections, including ear infections, sinus infections, throat infections (strep throat), bronchitis, pneumonia, urinary tract infections (UTIs), and some skin infections. It works by killing the bacteria causing your infection. It does NOT work for viral infections like the cold or flu.
how_to_take: Take cefpodoxime by mouth with food to help your body absorb it better and to reduce stomach upset. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. If you are taking the liquid (oral suspension), shake the bottle well before each use and measure your dose carefully with the measuring spoon or syringe that came with the medicine — do not use a regular kitchen spoon. Take every dose at evenly spaced times and finish ALL of your medicine, even if you start feeling better before it is gone. Stopping too soon can allow the infection to come back.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your age, weight, kidney function, and the type of infection being treated. Common adult doses range from 100 mg to 400 mg taken every 12 hours (twice a day) for 5 to 14 days. For children, the dose is based on body weight and is usually given twice a day. Always follow the exact dose and schedule your doctor prescribed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one, as this could increase your risk of side effects.
storage: Tablets: Store at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep away from heat, light, and moisture. Do not store in the bathroom. Liquid suspension: After mixing, store in the refrigerator. Do not freeze. Use within 14 days and throw away any remaining liquid after that time. Keep all forms of this medication out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking antacids that contain aluminum or magnesium (such as Maalox or Mylanta) or medicines that reduce stomach acid (such as famotidine or omeprazole) at the same time as cefpodoxime, as they can reduce how well the antibiotic is absorbed into your body. If you must take these medicines, ask your pharmacist or doctor for guidance on timing. Avoid alcohol while taking antibiotics, as it may worsen side effects like stomach upset. Do not share this medication with others, even if they have similar symptoms.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek emergency medical help right away if you experience: a severe allergic reaction (rash, hives, itching, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, trouble breathing, or dizziness); severe diarrhea that is watery or bloody, or stomach cramps (this could be a serious gut infection called C. diff); yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); dark urine; unusual bruising or bleeding; or seizures. Also call your doctor if your infection does not seem to be improving after a few days, or if it gets worse.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within 2 to 3 days of starting cefpodoxime. However, it is very important to keep taking all of your medicine for the full number of days prescribed, even if your symptoms improve. The infection may not be completely cleared if you stop early, and bacteria could become resistant to the antibiotic.
special_populations: Kidney problems: If you have kidney disease, your doctor may lower your dose or have you take it less often, since this drug is removed from the body through the kidneys. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Cefpodoxime is generally considered relatively safe during pregnancy and passes into breast milk in small amounts, but your doctor should help decide if it is right for you. Children: This medicine can be used in children, and the liquid form is available for those who cannot swallow tablets. Older adults: No special dose changes are usually needed unless you also have kidney problems. Penicillin allergy: Tell your doctor if you are allergic to penicillin antibiotics, as there is a small chance of cross-reaction with cephalosporins like cefpodoxime.
